645.title: Rosh Hashanah: kingship, memory, shofar
645.hook: the extra service has three parts: God as king, God remembering, the shofar
645.howItsDone: In the Rosh Hashanah Musaf, the prayer leader recites Malchuyot, Zichronot and Shofarot, each with ten verses, and in many synagogues the shofar is sounded after each; many congregations kneel and bow to the floor at Aleinu.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the world's birthday. Your line was happy birthday, world. Today, the heart of the Rosh Hashanah service, in three parts.

On most Shabbats and festivals, the additional Amidah, the Musaf, has seven blessings. On Rosh Hashanah it has nine. The three in the middle are each built like a small anthology: ten verses chosen from across the Bible, stitched into a prayer, and followed, in many synagogues, by the shofar. Ever sat through a Rosh Hashanah service and wondered why it's so long? This is a big part of the answer.
screen: `SEVEN BLESSINGS BECOME NINE.` → `TEN VERSES EACH.` → `WHY IT'S SO LONG.`

segments.voice: The three middle blessings are Malchuyot, kingship; Zichronot, remembrances; and Shofarot, the shofar. The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 16a, explains them as if God were speaking: say before Me kingships, so that you make Me king over you; remembrances, so that your memory rises before Me for good. And how? With the shofar. The Mishnah asks for ten verses for each. In the prayer book they're drawn from the Torah, the Writings and the Prophets, ending with the Torah again. One Malchuyot verse comes from the Song of the Sea: "The LORD shall reign for ever and ever." The prayer that opens Malchuyot is Aleinu, our duty to praise, the one that ends every daily service. Tradition says it began here, as the introduction to kingship on Rosh Hashanah, and only later moved into the everyday. On Rosh Hashanah, at the words we bend the knee, many congregations don't just bow. They kneel, and bow to the floor. Why start the new year with kingship? In the old world, a king was the one whose word ruled your days. To say God is king is to ask: what actually rules my life? My phone. My fear. My boss. The approval of people I don't even like. Malchuyot is a yearly audit of loyalties. Before the tradition asks God to remember you, it asks you to decide whom you serve.
screen: `KINGSHIP, MEMORY, SHOFAR.` · `MAKE ME KING OVER YOU.` · `TEN VERSES, THREE KINDS OF BOOK.` · `ALEINU BEGAN HERE.` · then, large: `WHO IS KING?`

segments.voice: Be honest about what actually sets your schedule, your mood and your choices, and name two or three things without judging them; some may be good, a child, a calling, and some may not. Then ask what you'd want to rule your days if you could choose. If you pray, you can say the line from the Song of the Sea, the LORD shall reign; if not, name the value you'd crown.
Malchuyot. Kingships. The first of the three great middle blessings of the Rosh Hashanah Musaf, where God is declared king.
Your line: who is king. Kingship first, then memory, and only then the shofar. Until tomorrow.

646.title: Rosh Hashanah: the three sounds
646.hook: tekiah, shevarim, teruah: one long blast, broken sighs, short sobs
646.howItsDone: On Rosh Hashanah (except on Shabbat) the shofar is sounded in the synagogue in sets of tekiah, shevarim and teruah, a caller announcing each note; many communities reach one hundred blasts over the service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malchuyot, kingship, the yearly audit. Your line was who is king. Today, the sound the third blessing calls for.

Stand in a synagogue on Rosh Hashanah and listen. A man lifts a curved horn to his lips. A caller beside him reads out a word, and he blows one long, steady note. Another word, and the horn makes three broken, wavering notes, like someone catching their breath. A third word, and a rapid string of short bursts, almost a stammer. Then one long note again. Three kinds of sound, over and over, and by a custom many keep, a hundred blasts by the end of the day.
screen: `ONE LONG, STEADY NOTE.` → `THREE BROKEN NOTES.` → `A STRING OF SHORT BURSTS.`

segments.voice: The three sounds are tekiah, the long blast; shevarim, the broken notes, from a word meaning breaks; and teruah, the rapid short ones. The Torah calls Rosh Hashanah a day of teruah, but it never describes what a teruah sounds like. So the Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 33b and 34a, investigates. It notices that the old Aramaic translation renders teruah with a word for crying, and it finds the same root in the Song of Deborah, where Sisera's mother waits at her window for a son who will never come home, and cries. So a teruah is a cry. But what kind? Maybe a groan: long, heavy sighs. Maybe a wail: short, gasping sobs. Maybe both, sighs and then sobs, the way people really cry. Nobody could be sure which the Torah meant. So the sage Rabbi Abbahu, in Caesarea, set an order that covered every possibility: the sighs alone, the sobs alone, and the sighs followed by the sobs, each with a long, steady tekiah before and after. That's why the pattern is so long and adds up to so many blasts: the tradition wasn't certain, so it chose to do every version. Notice the frame, too. The broken sounds always sit inside the whole ones: crying, held on both sides by something steady. Many teachers read it as a picture of the year. The brokenness is real, and it is not the whole story.
screen: `TEKIAH, SHEVARIM, TERUAH.` · `A DAY OF TERUAH, NEVER DESCRIBED.` · `SISERA'S MOTHER AT THE WINDOW.` · `SIGHS, SOBS, OR BOTH.` · then, large: `A SIGH AND A SOB.`

segments.voice: Breathe the pattern slowly: one long, steady breath out like a tekiah, three breaths out in pieces like sighs, a few quick short ones like sobs, then one long, whole breath again. If something from this year needs a sigh, let it have one, and if you pray, let the breaths carry it to God. The long breath at the end is there to hold the rest.
Teruah. The broken cry of the shofar, whose exact sound the Torah never describes, so the tradition plays every version.
Your line: a sigh and a sob. With a long, steady note on either side. Day six hundred forty-six.

647.title: Rosh Hashanah: Hannah (1 Samuel 1)
647.hook: the haftarah tells of Hannah praying for a child, and being heard
647.tomorrow: Rosh Hashanah: the boy is heard (Genesis 21)
647.howItsDone: On the first day of Rosh Hashanah, after the Torah reading, the haftarah from 1 Samuel 1:1–2:10 is chanted in the synagogue, including Hannah's prayer and her song of thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three sounds of the shofar. Your line was a sigh and a sob. Today, a woman the rabbis learned to pray from, read on the new year.

Every year the family goes up to the sanctuary at Shiloh for a festive meal, and every year it's the same scene. Elkanah gives portions of meat to his wife Peninnah and all her sons and daughters. To his other wife, Hannah, whom he loves, he gives a double portion, because Hannah has no children. And every year, Peninnah makes sure she feels it. Hannah cries and won't eat. Her husband asks, gently and a bit cluelessly: "am not I better to thee than ten sons?"
screen: `EVERY YEAR, UP TO SHILOH.` → `A DOUBLE PORTION, NO CHILDREN.` → `BETTER THAN TEN SONS?`

segments.voice: This is the haftarah, the prophetic reading, for the first day of Rosh Hashanah: the first chapter of Samuel. Weeks ago you met Hannah's quiet prayer, lips moving with no voice, which the rabbis made the model for the Amidah. Today's question is why her story is read on the new year. The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 11a, says that on Rosh Hashanah three women were remembered: Sarah, Rachel and Hannah, three women who had longed for children. So on the day the liturgy is full of remembrance, the reading is about a woman who asked to be remembered, almost in those words. Her vow says: if Thou wilt "remember me, and not forget Thy handmaid." Watch what Hannah does. She doesn't argue with Peninnah, and she doesn't accept her husband's comfort as an answer. She gets up from the table, goes to the sanctuary, and pours out her soul. When the priest Eli thinks she's drunk, she corrects him, respectfully and firmly, and he blesses her. The text says her face was no more sad. Before anything has changed, she's already lighter. In time she has a son, Samuel, and here's the turn: she gives him back, bringing him to serve at Shiloh. The next chapter is her song of thanks, about reversals: the Lord brings low and lifts up, the barren bears seven. Being heard, for Hannah, began before the answer came. It began with being seen.

segments.voice: Let yourself name something you long for, not a small want but something you've carried, maybe for years, maybe quietly, the way Hannah got up from the table and named hers. If you pray, pour it out to God in your own words, lips moving if you like; if not, say it to yourself honestly, without needing an answer. Notice whether naming it changes how you sit.

648.title: Rosh Hashanah: the boy is heard (Genesis 21)
648.hook: the first day's reading includes Hagar and Ishmael rescued by a well
648.howItsDone: On the first day of Rosh Hashanah, Genesis 21, Isaac's birth and the rescue of Hagar and Ishmael, is read from the Torah scroll in the synagogue; the second day reads Genesis 22, the binding of Isaac.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the haftarah of Hannah. Your line was Hannah was heard. Today, the Torah reading of the same morning, and another mother crying.

The desert of Beer-sheba. A woman and her son, sent away from the only home he's known with some bread and a skin of water. The water runs out. The boy weakens. His mother lays him under one of the bushes, walks away about a bowshot, and sits down. She can't watch him die. She lifts up her voice and weeps. On the first morning of Rosh Hashanah, this is the story read aloud from the Torah.
screen: `THE DESERT OF BEER-SHEBA.` → `THE WATER RUNS OUT.` → `A BOWSHOT AWAY, SHE WEEPS.`

segments.voice: Genesis 21 begins with joy: Sarah, at last, gives birth to Isaac. The Talmud links that to Rosh Hashanah too: Sarah was remembered on this day. But the reading doesn't stop at the happy ending. It goes on to Hagar, Sarah's servant, and her son Ishmael, Abraham's firstborn, sent away into the wilderness. Then comes the verse at the center: "And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her: 'What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is.'" It's Hagar who weeps aloud, but the verse says God heard the boy, maybe his own quiet cry. And Ishmael's name means God hears, given before he was born, when Hagar first fled into the desert. Then God opens her eyes, and she sees a well of water she hadn't seen. The rabbis lingered on the words where he is. Rashi, drawing on the midrash, says the angels objected: this boy's descendants will one day cause harm. God answered: what is he right now? Right now, he's innocent. A person is judged as they are, where they are, today. On the day of judgment, that's the reading: not who you might become, not what your children might do. Ishmael is honored in Muslim tradition as well, as a prophet and an ancestor. Here, in the Jewish reading, he is simply a thirsty boy, and he is heard.

segments.voice: Think of someone outside your circle you don't usually think about, someone sent away, someone on the other side of a line, someone whose story isn't yours, and picture them where they are right now: thirsty, tired, or just living their day. If you pray, ask God to hear them, as the boy was heard; if not, wish them a well of water, whatever that means for them.

649.title: Rosh Hashanah: the books (Rosh Hashanah 16b)
649.hook: the Talmud pictures three books opened on the new year
649.howItsDone: From Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, Jews add lines to the Amidah asking to be remembered and written in the book of life, and greet each other with 'l'shanah tovah tikatevu' and later 'g'mar chatimah tovah.'

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hagar, Ishmael and the well. Your line was God hears the boy. Today, the picture behind a Rosh Hashanah greeting.

Leaving synagogue on Rosh Hashanah, people don't just say happy new year. They say: l'shanah tovah tikatevu, may you be written for a good year. Cards say it. Text messages say it. After Rosh Hashanah the greeting shifts: g'mar chatimah tovah, may you be sealed for good. Written. Sealed. It sounds like paperwork, and in a way it is. It comes from a single image in the Talmud: books lying open in heaven.
screen: `MAY YOU BE WRITTEN.` → `MAY YOU BE SEALED.` → `BOOKS LYING OPEN.`

segments.voice: In Rosh Hashanah 16b, Rabbi Kruspedai says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: three books are opened on Rosh Hashanah. One for the completely righteous, one for the completely wicked, and one for those in between, the beinonim. The completely righteous are written and sealed at once, for life. The completely wicked are written and sealed at once, for death. Those in between are held, suspended, from Rosh Hashanah until Yom Kippur: if they earn merit, they're written for life; if not, for death. Now be honest: how many people do you know who are completely righteous, or completely wicked? Almost everyone is in the middle book. That's the point of the image. The middle book is the open one, still being written, and the ten days ahead are for what goes in it. Maimonides, centuries later, turned this into advice. A person should see themselves all year as exactly half good and half not, he said, and the whole world the same way. Then any single good act could tip you, and the world, toward life. The prayers of these days come back to the image again and again: remember us for life, and write us in the book of life. Then they give a reason: for Your sake, living God. The request for life is made to the God of life. It's a frightening image, and it's meant to be. But it's also hopeful. The book isn't closed yet.

segments.voice: Write one sentence you'd want in the book about you a year from now, on a scrap of paper or in your phone's notes: not a resolution about the gym, but something like she was kinder to her brother, or he finally called his father. If you pray, you can ask to be written for a good year; if not, let the line be a direction.

Your line: write us in. Written on Rosh Hashanah, sealed on Yom Kippur. That's day six hundred forty-nine.

650.title: The ten days
650.hook: the days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are for making amends
650.howItsDone: During the Ten Days of Repentance, Jews change wording in the Amidah (HaMelech HaKadosh), say Avinu Malkeinu, add selichot, and many seek out people they have wronged to apologize before Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three books, and the middle one still open. Your line was write us in. Today, the days when that middle book is being written.

There's a particular feeling to the days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. The holiday food is in the fridge. Work and school have started again. Life looks ordinary, but people who keep these days describe a hum underneath, like the week before a big exam. Words in the daily prayers shift. Someone you haven't heard from in a year calls, a bit awkwardly, to say they're sorry.
screen: `LIFE LOOKS ORDINARY.` → `A HUM UNDERNEATH.` → `AN AWKWARD PHONE CALL.`

segments.voice: These are the aseret yemei teshuvah, the ten days of return, counting Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur themselves. The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 18a, reads a verse from Isaiah as being about these days: "Seek ye the LORD while He may be found, call ye upon Him while He is near." These are the near days. The daily Amidah changes to match. All year, one blessing ends: the holy God. For these ten days it ends: the holy King. Forget, and in many traditions you go back and say it again. Avinu Malkeinu, our father, our king, is said at many services, and some people take on stricter habits just for these days. At the center is teshuvah, usually translated repentance, though the word means return, turning back. Maimonides lays out what it involves. You recognize what you did wrong. You regret it. You say it out loud, in words, to God. And you resolve not to do it again. Then he gives a test for whether teshuvah is complete. You find yourself in the same situation, with the same temptation, the same person, the same chance, and this time you choose differently. Not because you can't. Because you've changed. That's the work of these days: not grand gestures but specific turns, one person, one habit, one sentence. Ten days is not long. Long enough to do something, short enough that it can't be put off.

651.title: The Shabbat of return (Hosea 14:2)
651.hook: the Shabbat between, with Hosea's "Return, O Israel"
651.howItsDone: On the Shabbat between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, the haftarah from Hosea 14 (with additions from Joel or Micah, by custom) is read, and many rabbis give a major sermon on teshuvah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, teshuvah and the ten days of return. Your line was ten days to turn. Today, the one Shabbat inside those ten days, and the end of a week.

Every year, between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, there's exactly one Shabbat. It has its own name, taken from the first word of its prophetic reading. In many communities the rabbi gives a long sermon that day, all about coming back. Otherwise it looks like any other Shabbat: candles, a long meal, an afternoon nap. And the reading opens with a single Hebrew word, shuvah. Return.
screen: `ONE SHABBAT BETWEEN.` → `A SERMON ABOUT COMING BACK.` → `SHUVAH: RETURN.`

segments.voice: Shabbat Shuvah is named for the haftarah from the prophet Hosea: "Return, O Israel, unto the LORD thy God; for thou hast stumbled in thine iniquity." Notice the word Hosea chooses. Not you have rebelled, not you are wicked. Stumbled. You tripped; you can get up. The next verse gives instructions, and they're surprising: "Take with you words, and return unto the LORD." Not sacrifices, not gold, not a grand gesture. Words. Hosea goes on: instead of bulls, we'll offer the words of our lips. Later rabbis leaned on this verse when the Temple was gone: prayer could stand in for the offerings. The reading ends in tenderness. God promises to heal, to love freely, to be like dew to Israel, so that it blossoms like a lily. Some call this day Shabbat Teshuvah, the Shabbat of repentance. Shuvah is the command form: come back. Much of the Days of Awe speaks the language of a court: judgment, books, seals. Shabbat Shuvah sounds more like a parent standing at the door. You stumbled. Come back. Bring words. On the day of rest itself, the whole season comes down to its simplest version: return.
screen: `SHUVAH: COME BACK.` · `YOU STUMBLED; YOU CAN GET UP.` · `TAKE WITH YOU WORDS.` · `LIKE DEW, LIKE A LILY.` · then, large: `RETURN.`

segments.voice: Think of one place where you stumbled this year, just one, and take Hosea's advice: find the words you'd say if you were coming back, and say them quietly in your own language, to God if you pray, or to yourself as someone who can get up. Then breathe, and picture dew on grass in the morning.
Shabbat Shuvah. The Shabbat of return, between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, named for Hosea's call: return, O Israel.
